bullets: How to name angles by size, measure them with a protractor, and add them on lines, at a point, and in triangles
slides.heading: Angles: identify, measure, add
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we learn to spot right, acute and obtuse angles, measure with a protractor, and add angles that sit on a straight line, at a point, and inside a triangle - and by the end you will be able to explain why longer arms do not make a bigger angle.

bullets: Name an angle by its size: acute is under 90 degrees, right is exactly 90, obtuse is over 90
Measure an angle with a protractor: centre on the vertex, baseline on one arm
Add angles: 180 degrees on a straight line, 360 at a point, 180 inside a triangle
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: Two angles are both 45 degrees, but one is drawn with much longer arms
A classmate says the one with longer arms must be the bigger angle - is that right?
slides.heading: Does a bigger drawing mean a bigger angle?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: is the long-armed angle bigger, or are they equal? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s5 settles this exactly.

bullets: An angle is the turn between two arms that meet at a vertex
Only the size of the turn matters - the lengths of the arms do not change the angle
slides.heading: An angle measures a turn, not a length
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: an angle is a turn, measured in degrees, and arm length never changes it.

bullets: A right angle is exactly 90 degrees; smaller than that is acute, bigger is obtuse
60 degrees is acute, 90 is right, and 120 is obtuse
slides.heading: Right, acute, obtuse — spot the size
slides.notes: Narrate the moving arm as it swings: under 90 the angle is acute, at exactly 90 it is right, and past 90 it turns obtuse.

bullets: Line the protractor centre dot up with the vertex, and the baseline with one arm
Read where the other arm crosses the scale - that number is the angle
slides.heading: Measuring with a protractor
slides.notes: Work the measuring slowly: centre on the vertex first, baseline along one arm, then read the scale where the second arm crosses it.

bullets: Two angles sharing a straight line always add to 180 degrees
A full spin around one point is 360 degrees
slides.heading: Angles on a straight line, angles at a point
slides.notes: Point at the straight line first: the two angles fill a half-turn, 180 degrees; then the full turn around a point, 360 degrees.

bullets: Tear the three corners off any triangle and they fit exactly onto a straight line: 180 degrees
The four corners of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees, and in a parallelogram opposite angles match
slides.heading: Triangle angle sum, quadrilateral corners
slides.notes: Narrate the torn corners lining up on the straight line: every triangle hides the same 180-degree total, whatever its shape.

bullets: Careful - the trap is judging an angle by the drawing: The angle with longer arms is bigger.
Same turn, same angle: a 45-degree angle stays 45 degrees however long its arms are drawn
slides.heading: Misconception: longer arms, same angle
slides.notes: Hold the claim up against the two drawings: the arms grew, but the turn between them never changed, so the angle is still 45 degrees.

bullets: Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees, so the missing angle is 180 - 65
Answer: 115 degrees - check: 115 + 65 = 180, so the line is complete
slides.heading: Worked example: the missing angle on a straight line
slides.notes: Talk through the adding slowly as in scene s3 and name each step as you write it; say: checking 115 + 65 = 180 keeps the working honest.

bullets: Name each angle as acute, right or obtuse, then measure it with your protractor
A triangle has angles of 90 and 40 degrees - find the third angle and show the working
slides.heading: Your turn: name, measure and add
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the protractor steps first, then on using the 180-degree triangle total.

bullets: On your own: find the missing angle on a straight line and show the working
Explain in one sentence why longer arms do not make a bigger angle
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the adds-to-180 working in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about the turn between the arms in your second.
